candidates.title: Maybelline rewrites its 35-year-old tagline: 'Maybe she's born with it. Maybe it's Maybelline.' becomes 'Maybe. We're born with it. Maybe. It's Maybelline.' Two full stops and one pronoun spark a social storm

sources.claim: PeakMetrics: mentions on X, Reddit, TikTok, Instagram peaked at 68x typical volume two days after debut; sentiment 48% negative, 28% positive, 24% neutral; ~a quarter object to wording/punctuation; 38% jokes or sarcasm; 59% framed it as forced inclusivity or political messaging. Copywriter quoted: 'It's so confusing.'
'Four sentences where there used to be two'; brand president Sandrine Jolly (via WWD): the original was 'giving ambiguity – it was more of a question.'

Tagline in use since 1991; punctuation makes it 'more like a declaration'; 'we're' replaces 'she's' to include all women; change is permanent; platform 'The Beauty of Infinite Possibility' with Miley Cyrus.
Allen Adamson: 'It's such an iconic set of words, and so hardwired to Maybelline that they can't walk away from it.'
Official: 'At Maybelline, "Maybe" means possibility.' H1 'MAYBE. WE'RE BORN WITH IT.'
'One word, two dots and a storm online'; notes early negative sentiment is not proof of sales effect.

'Social media users were quick to criticize'; cites NYT (Jared Watson, NYU Stern) and Forbes ('polarizing'); some critics wondered if AI wrote it; original first heard in a Finish Matte ad with Christy Turlington (per Forbes).

candidates.classification: breaking -> emerging (controversy, verified by social-listening data reported in 2 outlets)

lenses.verification_red_team: C1 facts agree across Marketing Dive, Marketing Brew, Creative Bloq, B&T, MediaPost and the official page. The 68x / 48% numbers are PeakMetrics data reported by Marketing Brew (and re-cited by Fashion Biznes), not independently audited: say 'one social-listening firm counted' if used. No sales effect is known; do not claim it failed commercially. 1991 = first use per sources (MediaPost/Forbes attribute first airing to a Finish Matte ad); do not name the writer (no source). 59% of negative posts framed it politically: do NOT take a political side; the reel's angle is copy craft (rhythm, ambiguity), and that framing is stated as a minority-of-the-story fact only in the caption if at all. Risk of overlap with 11-25 ('kept the name, changed the meaning'): angle tomorrow is different — editing a line people can sing, and the doubt that was the asset.
lenses.audience_psychology: Everyone can hum the line, in Persian- and English-speaking markets alike (Maybelline is widely sold and advertised in both). Curiosity gap: 'two dots made millions angry.' Shareable: people will test reading it aloud. Mild humour fits the voice (Creative Bloq: 'hostage reading out a statement').
lenses.brand_fit: Pure brand strategy and copywriting: slogan equity, distinctive assets, sound and rhythm, when to update a legacy line. Gives business owners a concrete rule: before 'fixing' your famous line, find out what people actually remember about it. Passes the gate; no private individuals; Miley Cyrus not shown.

gates.brand_fit: C1 pass, C2 pass, C3 pass (but AI overlap), C4 fail (repeat AI + Coke within 14 days), C9 fail (repeat Black Friday)
gates.story: C1 has the strongest central tension (the line worked because it was a question; the brand turned it into a statement) and the most concrete image (two full stops; a mascara wand drawing a dot). C2 has a strong image (cream jar in sand) but weak tension and no virality evidence.

winner.why: Highest score (90/100 estimate), verified social-listening evidence, global recognition, fresh (launched 10 Nov, reaction through 17 Nov), and a lesson every business owner can use. Runner-up: C2 CeraVe x Dune (77) — keep for nearer the 18 Dec release.
